question: In the plenary debate on the European Democracy Shield on 18 December 2025, Commissioner McGrath referred to ‘evidence before our eyes’ of foreign interference in elections, including in Romania. The Commission has since opened formal proceedings under the Digital Services Act (DSA) concerning ‘systemic risks linked to election integrity’ in the Romanian presidential elections.

By contrast, in the case of the arrest of Telegram founder Pavel Durov, the Commission has stated, in its reply to written question E-003878/20251 and through its spokespeople, that the matter is purely national and is unrelated to the DSA. 1.

Given that both situations involve the alleged misuse of online communications during electoral periods, can the Commission specify the objective criteria it applies to determine when alleged interference triggers EU-level DSA enforcement, and when it does not?
Does the Commission maintain a written methodology for assessing when an electoral context constitutes a ‘systemic risk’ under Articles 34-35 DSA, and will it publish this to ensure legal certainty?
How does the Commission ensure consistency and avoid politically sensitive or platform-size-based discretion in deciding which cases merit EU-level intervention?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.2.2026) Telegram’s founder faces criminal proceedings in France, based on the French Criminal Code, and not in relation to the Digital Services Act (DSA). The Commission does not comment on national investigations.

Furthermore, Telegram is not designated as very large online platform under the DSA, and, therefore, the Commission has no competence to initiate proceedings under this regulation against the company. That competence lies with Belgian digital services coordinator, BIPT.

To protect the integrity of elections, under the DSA, very large online platforms (‘VLOPs’) and very large search engines (‘VLOSEs’) are obliged to diligently assess and mitigate any systemic risks stemming from the design or functioning of their service and its related systems, including any actual or foreseeable negative effects on electoral processes.

In April 2024, the Commission issued guidelines for VLOPs and VLOSEs on the mitigation of systemic risks for electoral processes, which recommend various mitigation measures1. Under the DSA, the Commission may initiate a proceeding against any VLOP or VLOSE if suspected of having infringed any of the provisions of the DSA, for instance against TikTok in December 20242.
The Commission must respect the Charter of Fundamental Rights, including the principle of non-discrimination. Any DSA-related decision can be challenged before the Court of Justice of the EU.
